name: UniOme
tagline: A local-first annotation browser for prokaryotes — genes, structures, interactions, regulation and pathways, served entirely from files on your own machine.
summary: UniOme brings together the annotation you would otherwise chase across a dozen web databases — per-gene annotation, protein and RNA structure and features, interactions, regulation and pathways — and puts it in one browser that runs on your own machine. There is no database server to install and no network round-trip: everything is served from local files.

Four organisms ship today: Escherichia coli K-12, Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv, Staphylococcus aureus NCTC 8325 and Bacillus subtilis 168. More are added over time, and the data-build scripts live in the repository so a new organism can be ported.

highlights.title: Around 30 databases, one interface
highlights.body: Annotation integrated from roughly thirty external biological databases, cross-linked per gene instead of scattered across separate sites.

highlights.title: Works offline
highlights.body: No database server, no account and no network dependency — the datasets ship with the app and are read straight from disk.

highlights.title: Structure and features in context
highlights.body: Protein and RNA structure and features sit alongside the interactions, regulation and pathway data for the same gene.

highlights.title: Provenance you can audit
highlights.body: Every dataset's origin, licence and primary citation is documented, so you can tell where any given value came from.

os.macOS: Apple silicon (arm64) or Intel (x64) — packaged builds
os.Other: Runs from source on any OS with Node.js

hardware.Disk: Several GB — the datasets ship with the app

citation.text: yjzhng (2026). UniOme: a local-first annotation-database browser for prokaryotes. Version 0.1.0. https://github.com/yjzhng/UniOme

name: prokDB
tagline: Build one merged gene-annotation table for any prokaryote — NCBI, UniProt and KEGG integrated by a seven-step pipeline, as a desktop app or a command line.
summary: prokDB takes a tax ID and returns a single annotation table for that organism, merging NCBI RefSeq and GenBank genome features, UniProt protein annotation and KEGG pathways and families into one CSV — with optional subcellular localisation predicted locally by DeepLocPro.

The desktop app is a front end for the same seven-step pipeline you can run from the command line, sharing one output tree. Steps can be run individually or all at once, completed steps are detected from the files on disk, and the finished database can be previewed — sorted, filtered and paged — without leaving the window.

highlights.title: Four annotation sources, one table
highlights.body: NCBI RefSeq and GenBank, UniProt and KEGG merged per gene, with a stable local ID and a documented column for every source.

highlights.title: Nothing to install first
highlights.body: On first launch the app fetches its own CPython and the pipeline's packages via uv, all inside its own directory — no conda, no system Python.

highlights.title: Localisation predicted on your machine
highlights.body: DeepLocPro predicts prokaryotic subcellular localisation locally, adding a localz column to the merged database.

highlights.title: Resumable, and scriptable
highlights.body: Runs skip any step whose output already exists, so an interrupted build picks up where it stopped; batch mode takes a CSV of organisms in one go.

os.Other: Runs from source on any OS with Node.js 20+

hardware.Disk: Space for the private Python environment and each organism's output
hardware.Network: Needed to set up on first launch and to query the annotation sources

name: ChemSketcher
tagline: Draw a molecule and watch its physicochemical properties compute live — an open-source sketchpad with an RDKit property table built in.
summary: ChemSketcher is a desktop molecule sketchpad built on EPAM Ketcher, paired with an interactive table that computes physicochemical properties with RDKit as you draw. Sketch a structure or paste a SMILES string and the numbers appear beside it, with no round-trip to a web service.
Every distinct molecule on the canvas is recognised automatically and gets its own row, so you can compare a series side by side while you are still drawing it.

highlights.title: Properties as you draw
highlights.body: SMILES, molecular weight, logP, TPSA, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, ring counts, QED and InChIKey, computed live by RDKit.

highlights.title: Each molecule found automatically
highlights.body: Draw several structures on one canvas and each distinct molecule is detected and given its own row in the table.

highlights.title: Reads and writes the usual formats
highlights.body: Open and save .mol, .sdf, .ket and .smi files directly, so it fits whatever your pipeline already uses.

highlights.title: A layout you control
highlights.body: Choose which properties to show, move or hide the table, and drag the divider to give the canvas the room it needs.

os.macOS: Apple silicon (arm64) or Intel (x64) — packaged builds
os.Other: Runs from source on any OS with Node.js

hardware.Disk: ~1 GB for the bundled chemistry engine

name: ChemViewer
tagline: Explore chemical libraries interactively — compound properties, distribution statistics and side-by-side comparison, all computed locally.
summary: ChemViewer opens a chemical library and lets you actually look at it: browse compounds in a virtualised table, inspect property distributions across the whole set, and compare one library against another. Depiction, descriptors and substructure search all run locally through RDKit's WebAssembly build.

It is built to stay light on a laptop. Small libraries are held in memory; anything over about 50 MB is queried on disk with DuckDB instead, and large sets are subsampled before analysis — with an option to compute full statistics when you want them.

highlights.title: Reads the formats you already have
highlights.body: CSV, SDF, SMILES and CXSMILES — drop the files into a folder named after the library and it appears.

highlights.title: Large files without the wait
highlights.body: Libraries over 50 MB are queried on disk via DuckDB rather than loaded into memory, so opening one does not stall your machine.

highlights.title: See the whole library, not just rows
highlights.body: Property statistics, UMAP embedding plots, and library-versus-library comparison alongside the compound table.

highlights.title: Sketch to search
highlights.body: An embedded Ketcher canvas lets you draw a substructure and filter the library by it.

os.Other: Intel Macs and other OSes: run from source with Node.js

hardware.Memory: 8 GB — libraries under 50 MB are held in memory
hardware.Disk: Space for your libraries, plus dependencies
